member.name: T:OpenIGI.Platform.Desktop.DesktopConsole
member.summary: Connects a windowed game to the terminal it was started from, if any.

remarks.para: On Windows the game is a windowed (WinExe) program, so starting it never opens a console window of its own. That also means Windows gives it no console at all: started from a terminal, its output would go nowhere. borrows the parent's console in that case, so a capture or soak run from a shell still prints its log. When the output is already redirected — a launcher reading it, a script piping it to a file — the inherited handles are used as they are.
On macOS and Linux a program always has its parent's streams, and none of this applies.

The other two take the requested size, falling back to the monitor's when none was given. member.name: T:OpenIGI.Platform.Desktop.DesktopFramePacer
member.summary: Holds a loop to a target frame rate by waiting out the remainder of each frame's interval, for the menu, which renders uncapped and has nothing to gain past the display's own rate.

remarks.para: A menu that renders as fast as the machine can pegs the GPU at full load for a picture that changes only as fast as the display shows it. That costs heat and noise for nothing, and it costs something visible too: with the queue always full, the small uploads the menu does between frames -- a backdrop's residency, a preview being adopted -- land as hitches, because there is no slack for them to land in.
The wait is a sleep for the coarse part and a spin for the last stretch, because a bare sleep on Windows is granted in whole scheduler ticks and would overshoot by up to one.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Platform.Desktop.Logging.FileSink
member.summary: Writes records to a log file from a background thread, keeping the previous sessions' files beside it.

remarks.para: Desktop only: a browser has no file to write and no thread to write it from. The thread that logs only queues the record. The writer thread formats it, and flushes to disk every time the queue runs dry, so the file is never more than a moment behind the game. That matters most when the process dies without unwinding — an access violation inside a graphics driver — which is exactly the run a log is wanted for. waits for the queue to drain.

Opening a log rotates the earlier ones: runtime.log becomes runtime.1.log, and so on, up to the number kept. When another process is still writing the file — a second copy run for a capture or a comparison — rotation is impossible, so this session writes runtime.<pid>.log beside it instead.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Platform.Desktop.SilkGameWindow
member.summary: A desktop game window backed by Silk.NET windowing, with its input events fed into an .

remarks.para: The window is created and initialised eagerly so that exists before the caller builds a graphics device against it. It does not run Silk's own render loop: the game loop owns the frame, exactly as the original's WinMain message loop does, and is the message pump. Presentation belongs to the device's swapchain, so there is no present callback for the window to offer.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Platform.Desktop.SilkGameWindow.#cctor
member.summary: Names the windowing and input backend, rather than leaving Silk to go looking.

remarks.para: Silk finds its platforms by reflecting over the assemblies it can see, and a SINGLE-FILE publish takes that away: the backend assemblies are bundled inside the executable rather than sitting beside it, nothing enumerates them, and fails with "Couldn't find a suitable window platform" before a frame is drawn. The game builds and runs perfectly from a normal output directory and cannot start at all from a published one, which is a difference that only shows up at the very end.

Registering the backend by name is the documented answer and costs nothing in the ordinary case — it is the same platform the search would have found. Input needs saying separately from windowing; registering only the window leaves the mouse and keyboard dead in the same builds.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Platform.Desktop.SilkGameWindow.NoVulkanLoaderMessage
member.summary: What to say when no Vulkan loader could be opened at all.
member.remarks: Worth spelling out per platform, because the fix is completely different on each and the failure looks identical. On macOS there is no system Vulkan to be missing: the loader is MoltenVK, which the build carries under the one name GLFW will dlopen. GLFW then looks in exactly two places for it -- the working directory, and the bundle's Contents/Frameworks -- so this is a build started from somewhere neither of them names.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Platform.Desktop.SilkGameWindow.SupportsRawMouseMotion
member.summary: Gets whether a locked cursor reports the sensor's own counts rather than accelerated ones.
member.remarks: This is what makes the look a fixed number of radians per mouse count. Without it the lock falls back to an ordinary hidden-and-captured cursor, the desktop's pointer ballistics stay in the path, and slow movements are scaled toward zero before they ever reach the game — which is the classic "small movements do not register" of a mouse look. Reported rather than silently accepted, because the difference is invisible from inside the game and impossible to guess from outside it.

member.summary: An icon in the Windows notification area, with a menu, that also shows the program's notifications.

remarks.para: GLFW has no notion of the notification area, so this talks to the shell directly. It owns a message-only window, created on the thread that runs the program's event loop, so the clicks the shell sends it arrive through that loop's own event wait, with nothing else to pump. A left click raises ; a right click opens the menu. When Explorer restarts, the icon is put back.
Windows only: GLFW gives macOS and Linux nothing equivalent, and a program there minimises to the Dock or the taskbar instead.
